design_goal: Make every combat terminal teach a real coding strategy and validate behavior with visible and hidden tests.
schema_note: Entries carry both the loader's shared fields (id,title,language,concept,difficulty,strategies,common_mistakes) and forward-compatible learning fields (tier,micro_lesson,worked_example,prompt,starter,visible_tests,hidden_tests,misconceptions,world_effect,post_solve). world_effect binds the learner's OUTPUT to the in-world rescue (intrinsic integration). | 2026-07-04 item25: tiers 6-10 deepened to full 6-language depth (24 entries, generic-harness compatible).

entries.title: Java: methods and return values
strategies: Start with the method signature required by the mission.
Return the calculated value instead of printing from inside the method unless the prompt asks for printing.
Use small visible tests first, then check edge cases such as zero and negative values.
common_mistakes: Changing the method name expected by the hidden tests.
Printing the answer instead of returning it.

entries.title: Java: boolean access logic
strategies: Translate the English rule into truth-table language before coding.
Use && when every safety condition must be true.
Test true/true, true/false, false/true, and false/false.
common_mistakes: Using || when the rule requires all conditions.
Testing only the success case and missing unsafe false cases.
Confusing assignment with comparison in conditional expressions.

entries.title: C: functions, prototypes, and main
strategies: Include the needed headers before calling standard library functions.
Keep the function name and parameter order exactly as the harness expects.
Return an int from main and compile with warnings enabled.
common_mistakes: Returning a value from the wrong function.
Changing a test harness function name.

entries.title: Python: pure functions and readable tests
strategies: Keep mission functions pure when possible: same inputs should produce same outputs.
Use descriptive parameter names that match the rescue system.
Test the visible case and at least two hidden-style cases.
common_mistakes: Printing when the mission requires return.
Assuming truthy/falsy values without checking exact expected results.

entries.title: MATLAB: function files and vector awareness
strategies: Make the function name match the file name when working in MATLAB.
Use clear variable names and end function blocks explicitly.
Prefer vectorized operations when the mission asks for array behavior.
common_mistakes: Using a function name that does not match the file name.
Using matrix operators when element-wise operators are required.
Testing only scalar values when the mission will later use arrays.

entries.title: Debugging: isolate syntax, logic, and test failures
strategies: First ask whether the code compiles or runs at all.
If it runs, compare expected output against actual output for the smallest test case.
Read hidden-test failures as clues about generality, not as punishment.
common_mistakes: Solving only the visible example instead of the general rule.

entries.title: Compute a shelter's power draw
entries.micro_lesson: A variable stores a value; an expression combines variables with operators to make a new value.
entries.prompt: Return the total power a shelter needs: floors multiplied by draw-per-floor.
strategies: Name the value you want, then build it from the inputs.
Multiplication is repeated addition: floors groups of draw-per-floor.
common_mistakes: Using + when the rule says 'per floor' (that is multiplication).
Returning nothing / printing instead of returning.
entries.world_effect: The shelter's generator spins up to exactly the wattage you computed; its windows light in sequence.
entries.post_solve: You turned two inputs into one derived value — the core of every program: data in, result out.

entries.title: Average two fuel readings
entries.micro_lesson: Integer vs. real division matters: averaging needs real (floating) division.
entries.prompt: Return the average of two fuel-tank readings.
misconceptions: uses integer division and loses the .5
strategies: Add first, then divide by 2.
Watch integer division in Java/C: cast or use a real type.
common_mistakes: Dividing only one of the two values.
entries.world_effect: Two fuel gauges merge into one steady needle on the depot readout.
entries.post_solve: You met a classic trap: integer vs. real division. Types change results.

entries.title: Airlock access rule
entries.micro_lesson: Combine conditions with AND when ALL must hold; the result is a single true/false.
entries.worked_example: hasKey=true AND powerOn=false -> false; both must be true.
entries.prompt: Return true only when the survivor has the key and the airlock has power.
misconceptions: opens when only one condition is true
strategies: Turn the English rule into a truth table before coding.
Use AND (&&) when every condition is required.
common_mistakes: Using || when the rule needs all conditions.
Missing the boundary case where power exactly equals 100.
entries.world_effect: The airlock cycles open the instant both conditions are met; the survivor slips through.
entries.post_solve: Boolean logic is rule systems in miniature — validators, permissions, and game state all start here.

entries.title: Two-person airlock consent
entries.micro_lesson: AND is the safe-choice operator when two independent approvals are required.
entries.prompt: Return true only when both rescue staff are ready to unlock the checkpoint.
misconceptions: uses OR for a two-person rule
strategies: Name the two required facts.
Make a four-row truth table.
Only the true/true row should open.
entries.world_effect: Two wall switches light at once before the checkpoint door unlocks.
entries.post_solve: The rule is small, but it is the same shape as real permission checks: every required condition must pass.

entries.title: Power plus keycard gate
entries.micro_lesson: A boolean function should return the rule itself, not a printed explanation.
entries.worked_example: keycard=true, backupPower=true -> true; keycard=true, backupPower=false -> false.
entries.prompt: Return true only when the keycard is present and backup power is online.
misconceptions: prints unlocked instead of returning true
strategies: Keep the signature exactly as shown.
Return the combined boolean expression.
Use the visible test before changing anything else.
entries.world_effect: The keycard reader and backup generator both turn green before the lock releases.
entries.post_solve: Returning a boolean lets the game system decide what to do next. That makes your code reusable.

entries.title: Safe-zone lockout
entries.micro_lesson: The fastest way to debug a boolean rule is to check every row of the truth table.
entries.worked_example: true/false and false/true are both blocked because one required fact is missing.
entries.prompt: Return true only for the one safe truth-table row: both inputs true.
strategies: Write TT, TF, FT, FF beside the code.
Make only TT return true.
Let every other row return false.
entries.world_effect: Four truth-table lamps audit the lock; only the all-clear row opens the safe-zone door.
entries.post_solve: Truth tables make invisible logic visible. The validator's hidden tests are just the rows you did not see first.

entries.title: Route authorization lock
entries.micro_lesson: A good boolean function is tiny, explicit, and easy to test.
entries.worked_example: authorized=true, routeClear=true -> true; every other pair -> false.
entries.prompt: Return true only when authorization is granted and the rescue route is clear.
misconceptions: returns a string instead of a boolean
strategies: Prefer one clear return expression.
Confirm that the return type is boolean-like for your language.
Use hidden-test thinking: one false input must block the route.
entries.world_effect: The route authorization panel draws one clean green line only when both safety signals agree.
entries.post_solve: Small boolean functions are building blocks for bigger rescue systems because they are easy to compose and test.

entries.title: Triage tag by severity
entries.micro_lesson: if / elif / else pick exactly one branch, in order; order matters.
entries.prompt: Return the triage color for a severity 0-10: >=8 RED, >=4 YELLOW, else GREEN.
misconceptions: branch order reversed so everything is GREEN
strategies: Check the most severe condition first.
Each boundary (8, 4) needs a deliberate test.
common_mistakes: Ordering branches low-to-high so high severities never reach RED.
Using separate ifs that overwrite each other.
entries.world_effect: Numbered triage pylons light red, amber, and green over the wounded as you classify them.
entries.post_solve: Ordered branches are the backbone of every rule engine; the order IS the logic.

entries.title: Count survivors on a floor
entries.micro_lesson: A loop repeats work; an accumulator variable carries a running total across iterations.
entries.prompt: Return the total survivors across a list of room counts.

starter.python:
def total_survivors(rooms):
    total = 0
    # loop and add each room
    return total

misconceptions: resets the accumulator inside the loop
returns inside the loop after one room
strategies: Initialize the total once, before the loop.
Add each element; return after the loop ends.
common_mistakes: Putting the return inside the loop (stops after one item).
entries.world_effect: A tally board over the stairwell ticks up to the exact headcount as you sweep each room.
entries.post_solve: Accumulation — one variable summarizing many — is how programs turn data into answers.

entries.title: Relay pulse (FizzBuzz)
entries.micro_lesson: The modulo operator (%) gives a remainder; use it to test divisibility inside a loop.
entries.prompt: Return 1..n where multiples of 3 are 'Fizz', of 5 'Buzz', of both 'FizzBuzz'.
strategies: Test %15 (both) FIRST, then %3, then %5.
Predict 3, 5, and 15 before you code the branch order.
entries.world_effect: The relay pylons flash their pattern down the block, re-opening the signal path in rhythm.
entries.post_solve: Branch order + modulo is a surprisingly deep pattern: it is rule precedence made concrete.

entries.title: Route even evac units, in order
entries.micro_lesson: Filtering keeps items that pass a test WHILE preserving their original order.
entries.prompt: Return only the even unit numbers, preserving order.
strategies: Walk the list once; append items that pass the test.
Preserve order — do not sort.
entries.world_effect: Even-numbered evac trucks pull out first, in the exact order your filter returned them.
entries.post_solve: This is the whole thesis: your output IS the rescue. Filtering preserves order — that is why triage lists stay stable.

entries.title: Keep the lane clear when no even units exist
entries.micro_lesson: A correct filter can return an empty collection; empty is a valid result, not a failure.
entries.worked_example: [1,3,5] -> [] because no value passes the even test.
entries.prompt: Return the even unit numbers. If no unit is even, return an empty result without inventing a fallback.
misconceptions: returns null/None instead of an empty result
treats empty input as an error
strategies: Start with an empty result.
Only add a value after it passes the test.
Return the result even when nothing was added.
common_mistakes: Returning the original list when no evens are found.
entries.world_effect: The boarding lane stays physically clear when your filter returns no even units.
entries.post_solve: Empty output is still output. The rescue system can trust it because your code made no false positives.

entries.title: Pull even units out of a noisy queue
entries.micro_lesson: Filtering is a one-pass keep/reject decision for each item in the queue.
entries.prompt: Return every even emergency unit from a mixed queue, keeping the original order.
misconceptions: keeps values by index instead of by value
strategies: Inspect every item in sequence.
Append matching items to a separate result.
Do not break after the first even value.
common_mistakes: Returning only the first even value.
Testing the position number instead of the unit number.
entries.world_effect: Three kept convoy markers roll forward while rejected odd units stay parked.
entries.post_solve: The queue was noisy, but the predicate stayed simple: every value got one fair keep/reject check.

entries.title: Filter even units with zero and negatives
entries.micro_lesson: Evenness is about divisibility by 2; zero and negative numbers can be even too.
entries.prompt: Return every even value, including zero and negative even unit IDs.
misconceptions: assumes only positive numbers can be even
uses greater-than checks instead of modulo
strategies: Use the same evenness test for every integer.
Do not add a positive-only guard.
Trace zero as a visible edge case.
common_mistakes: Rejecting zero even though it is divisible by 2.
Filtering positive numbers instead of even numbers.
entries.world_effect: Cold-storage units, reserve units, and unit zero enter the convoy only when the filter proves they are even.
entries.post_solve: Edge cases are where a concept becomes durable: the same predicate handled positive, negative, and zero.

entries.title: Preserve duplicate even units
entries.micro_lesson: Filtering is not deduping. If an even value appears twice, both appearances survive in order.
entries.prompt: Return every even unit occurrence, preserving duplicates and order.
strategies: Append every matching occurrence.
Avoid sets when the prompt asks for order.
Use the visible test to prove duplicates survive.
common_mistakes: Sorting duplicate values into a new order.
entries.world_effect: Duplicate even convoy slots remain visible so no survivor is silently dropped from the manifest.
entries.post_solve: Stable filtering respects the original queue. That is why every duplicate survivor slot is still represented.

entries.title: Strongest signal in the array
entries.micro_lesson: Track a 'best so far' variable, updating it as you scan.
entries.prompt: Return the maximum value in a non-empty list of signal strengths.
strategies: Initialize 'best' to the first element, not 0.
Compare each element and keep the larger.
common_mistakes: Assuming values are positive (0-init breaks negatives).
Returning the final element instead of the max.
entries.world_effect: The comms dish rotates to lock onto the single strongest beacon you identified.
entries.post_solve: 'Best so far' is a reusable pattern: max, min, closest, cheapest all share this shape.

entries.title: Reverse the door code
entries.micro_lesson: Strings are sequences you can index and walk backward.
entries.prompt: Return the reversed string of a door code.
strategies: Build the result from the last index down to the first.
Empty and single-char strings should just work.
entries.world_effect: The keypad re-sequences and the vault door rolls back along its track.
entries.post_solve: Indexing and boundaries are where most string bugs live; test empty and length-1 always.

entries.title: Reverse empty and single-letter codes
entries.micro_lesson: Boundary cases are not special failures: empty and one-character strings reverse to themselves.
entries.prompt: Return the reversed string while handling empty and one-character door codes.
misconceptions: starts at length instead of length-1
strategies: Start from the last valid index.
Let a zero-iteration loop return an empty result.
Test length 0, 1, and 2 before longer strings.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one on the first or last index.
Assuming every code has at least two characters.
entries.world_effect: The vault accepts a blank maintenance code without jamming, then confirms a one-letter code unchanged.
entries.post_solve: Boundary cases prove the loop is shaped correctly before the larger rescue code arrives.

entries.title: Reverse a radio signal token
entries.micro_lesson: A reverse copies characters from right to left while preserving every character exactly.
entries.prompt: Return the reversed radio token exactly, preserving all letters.
strategies: Append or assign each input character exactly once.
Trace the first output character: it must be the last input character.
Do not transform case or alphabetize.
common_mistakes: Sorting characters instead of reversing their positions.
Forgetting that repeated letters are separate positions.
entries.world_effect: Radio glyph tiles flip last-to-first until the rescue signal becomes readable.
entries.post_solve: Reverse is position work, not value work. Every character survives; only its location changes.

entries.title: Reverse mixed code digits
entries.micro_lesson: Digits inside a string are still characters; reverse their positions without doing arithmetic.
entries.prompt: Return the reversed mixed door code exactly, including digits.
strategies: Treat the whole input as a sequence of characters.
Move positions, not numeric values.
Check that digits reverse just like letters.
common_mistakes: Parsing digits instead of copying characters.
entries.world_effect: The keypad's numeric tumblers rotate into the reversed code order before the vault unlatches.
entries.post_solve: Strings can contain letters, digits, and symbols. Indexing code should preserve them all unless told otherwise.

entries.title: Reverse case-sensitive code
entries.micro_lesson: Reverse should preserve character identity; uppercase and lowercase characters stay exactly as they are.
entries.prompt: Return the reversed code while preserving uppercase and lowercase characters exactly.
misconceptions: compares letters instead of copying positions
strategies: Do not normalize case.
Copy exactly the character you read.
Use a mixed-case visible trace.
entries.world_effect: Uppercase and lowercase glyph plates slide into their reversed slots without changing color.
entries.post_solve: Preserving exact characters is how code keeps IDs, passwords, and rescue tokens trustworthy.

entries.title: Palindrome failsafe
entries.micro_lesson: A two-pointer walk compares the ends moving inward — linear and allocation-free.
entries.prompt: Return True if the string reads the same forwards and backwards.
misconceptions: compares only the first and last char
strategies: Move two pointers inward until they meet.
Empty and single-char are palindromes.
entries.world_effect: The failsafe recognizes the symmetric key and disarms the district's lockdown.
entries.post_solve: Two-pointer is a workhorse technique: palindromes, reversals, and merges all use it.

entries.title: Convert reactor temp
entries.micro_lesson: A function packages a computation behind a name; return hands the value back to the caller.
entries.prompt: Return Fahrenheit for a Celsius reactor reading.
misconceptions: applies operations in the wrong order
strategies: Follow the formula exactly; mind operator precedence.
Use real division so fractional degrees survive.
entries.world_effect: The reactor gauge re-labels itself in the survivor's units; the overheat alarm quiets.
entries.post_solve: Functions are reusable machines: name, inputs, one clear returned result.

entries.title: Clamp power to safe range
entries.micro_lesson: Small helper functions compose into larger logic; clamp keeps a value within bounds.
entries.prompt: Return value limited to the range [lo, hi].

starter.python:
def clamp(value, lo, hi):
    return value

strategies: Handle both the too-low and too-high cases.
Return the value untouched when already in range.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the lower OR upper bound.
entries.world_effect: The power regulator pins the grid to a safe ceiling; sparks stop arcing across the panel.
entries.post_solve: A tiny, well-named helper you can trust is worth more than clever one-off code.

entries.title: Cascade sequence (factorial)
entries.micro_lesson: Recursion solves a problem in terms of a smaller version, with a base case to stop.
entries.prompt: Return n! (n factorial). Assume n >= 0.
misconceptions: base case returns 0, zeroing the product
strategies: Write the base case first (n==0 -> 1).
Trust the recursive call for n-1, then combine.
entries.world_effect: Backup generators kick on in a cascading chain, each triggering the next down the grid.
entries.post_solve: Recursion is a mindset: solve the smallest case, then let the function trust itself.

entries.title: Relay handshake (Fibonacci)
entries.micro_lesson: Some recursions branch; recognizing repeated subproblems motivates memoization later.
entries.prompt: Return the nth Fibonacci number (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1).
misconceptions: adds the wrong two previous terms
strategies: Anchor both base cases (0 and 1).
fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2).
entries.world_effect: Two relay towers handshake in the classic spiral cadence, extending the signal chain.
entries.post_solve: Naive fib recomputes subproblems — a perfect setup for learning memoization next.

entries.title: District headcount board
entries.micro_lesson: A map/dictionary counts occurrences by key in one pass.
entries.prompt: Return a map from district label to the number of survivors tagged there.
strategies: For each label, add 1 to its running count.
Initialize a key to 0 the first time you see it.
common_mistakes: KeyError from reading a missing key.
entries.world_effect: The district board updates live, each neighborhood showing its exact rescued count.
entries.post_solve: Counting-by-key is one of the most useful patterns in real software — logs, votes, inventory.

entries.title: Locate survivor (binary search)
entries.micro_lesson: Binary search halves a SORTED range each step: O(log n) instead of O(n).
entries.prompt: Return the index of target in a sorted array, or -1 if absent.
misconceptions: infinite loop when mid never moves
strategies: Keep low<=high; move the bound past mid each step.
The array MUST be sorted for this to work.
common_mistakes: Using < instead of <= on the loop guard.
Not updating low/high, causing an infinite loop.
entries.world_effect: The roster scanner jumps straight to the survivor's bunk instead of checking every room.
entries.post_solve: Binary search is the payoff of sorted data: structure turns linear work into logarithmic work.

entries.title: Triage priority sort
entries.micro_lesson: Sorting reorders by a key; here, most-severe first (descending).
entries.prompt: Return the severities sorted from highest to lowest.
strategies: Sort, then reverse — or sort with a descending key.
Stable order for ties is fine.
common_mistakes: Ascending when the rule says highest-first.
Returning None after an in-place sort.
entries.world_effect: The triage line physically reorders: the most critical survivors move to the front of extraction.
entries.post_solve: Choosing the right key and direction is most of real-world 'sorting' — the algorithm is secondary.

entries.title: Evac manifest (capstone)
entries.micro_lesson: Real tasks compose primitives: filter, then sort, then remove duplicates — order of steps matters.
entries.prompt: From unit numbers, keep evens, order highest-first, and remove duplicates.
misconceptions: dedupes before sorting and loses order
strategies: Do it in stages: filter -> sort desc -> dedupe.
Test each stage on paper before combining.
common_mistakes: Forgetting one of the three operations.
entries.world_effect: The final extraction manifest prints clean: even units, priority order, no double-boarding.
entries.post_solve: Composition is the essence of programming: small correct pieces, assembled deliberately, solve big problems.

entries.title: Split the ration crates
entries.micro_lesson: The % (modulo) operator returns what remains after whole-number division — the classic 'how many are left over' tool.
entries.worked_example: 13 rations, 4 people -> each gets 3, 13 - 12 = 1 left over.
entries.prompt: Return how many rations remain after dividing them evenly among the survivors.
strategies: Trace one small example by hand first.
Remember: a % b is what's left AFTER a // b shares.
common_mistakes: Returning the quotient instead of the remainder.
entries.world_effect: The quartermaster stops double-counting; the spare crate glows for pickup.
entries.post_solve: Arithmetic operators are your first tools: / shares, % reports the remainder.

entries.title: Charge the generator
entries.micro_lesson: A loop repeats work; an accumulator variable carries the running total across iterations.
entries.prompt: Each crank i of the generator adds i units of charge. Return the total after n cranks.
strategies: Write the loop bounds for the smallest case (n=1) first.
Initialize total to 0 BEFORE the loop.
common_mistakes: Looping to n-1 and missing the last crank.
Resetting the total inside the loop.
entries.world_effect: The generator hums to life; corridor lights flicker on one by one.
entries.post_solve: Accumulation is THE loop pattern: initialize, update inside the loop, return after.

entries.title: Clamp the medkit dose
entries.micro_lesson: Functions take parameters, compute, and RETURN one result. Clamping = bounding a value into a range.
entries.worked_example: value=12, range 0..10 -> too high -> return the high bound, 10.
entries.prompt: Return the dose limited to the inclusive range [low, high].
misconceptions: returns a parameter instead of the clamped value
strategies: Handle 'too high' and 'too low' separately, then the pass-through case.
Test exactly at the bounds.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to return the unchanged value when in range.
entries.world_effect: The auto-injector stops overdosing; the medbay warning light turns green.
entries.post_solve: min/max composition beats if-chains: clamp(v) = max(low, min(high, v)).

entries.title: Fuel budget per kilometer
entries.micro_lesson: Real division keeps fractions. Returning a float lets callers do precise planning.
entries.prompt: Return how many liters the jeep burns per kilometer.
strategies: Keep units straight: liters PER km means liters / km.
Sanity-check with an easy pair like 1 L / 4 km.
common_mistakes: Rounding when the caller needs the exact rate.
entries.world_effect: The jeep's range readout switches from '??' to a real number the squad can trust.
entries.post_solve: Choose float types when the answer lives between whole numbers.

entries.title: Average the relay signals
entries.micro_lesson: Parameters are local names for the caller's values; combine them and return one summary.
entries.prompt: Return the mean strength of the three relay signals.
strategies: Sum first, divide once.
Use 3.0 so the division stays real.
common_mistakes: Dividing each term separately then adding.
entries.world_effect: The radio mast picks the strongest bearing; static clears from the channel.
entries.post_solve: A pure function of its parameters is trivial to test — that's why we live there.

entries.title: Curfew access window
entries.micro_lesson: A function can return a boolean directly — the comparison IS the answer; no if needed.
entries.prompt: The safehouse door opens from 08:00 inclusive to 18:00 exclusive. Return whether the given hour is inside the window.
strategies: Mark each bound inclusive/exclusive before coding.
Test both edges: 8 and 18.
common_mistakes: Combining with OR instead of AND.
entries.world_effect: The blast door's keypad glows green during the day cycle and red at night.
entries.post_solve: return (condition); beats if (condition) return true; else return false;.

entries.title: Countdown charge relay
entries.micro_lesson: Recursion = a base case that stops + a smaller call that shrinks toward it.
entries.prompt: Return n + (n-1) + ... + 1 using recursion (0 for n <= 0).
misconceptions: adds n-1 instead of n at each level
strategies: Write the base case FIRST and test it alone.
Trust the smaller call to be correct.
common_mistakes: Recursing on n instead of n-1.
Returning 1 at the base instead of 0.
entries.world_effect: Charge packets cascade down the relay tower and the beacon fires.
entries.post_solve: Every recursive solve is an induction proof you ran on a machine.

entries.title: Relay permutation lock
entries.micro_lesson: Factorial is the canonical recursion: n! = n * (n-1)!, with 1! = 1 as the floor.
entries.prompt: Return n! (n factorial) recursively; treat n <= 1 as 1.
misconceptions: base case returns 0 and zeroes everything
strategies: Identity for * is 1 — start there.
Trace n=2 fully before trusting n=6.
common_mistakes: Using n * factorial(n) and never shrinking.
entries.world_effect: The lock cycles through every wiring permutation and clicks open.
entries.post_solve: Multiplicative accumulation works exactly like additive — only the identity changes (1, not 0).

entries.title: Fibonacci beacon spacing
entries.micro_lesson: Some recursions branch twice: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), with TWO base cases.
entries.prompt: Return the n-th Fibonacci number (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1).
strategies: Pin BOTH base cases before the recursive line.
Check fib(2)=1 by hand.
entries.world_effect: Route beacons space themselves at nature's spacing; the column reads instantly at distance.
entries.post_solve: Branching recursion is powerful AND expensive — tier 10 shows you why (memoize!).

entries.title: Power-cell halving check
entries.micro_lesson: Recursive definition: 1 is a power of two; an even n is one iff n/2 is; everything else is not.
entries.prompt: Return whether n is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). n <= 0 is false.
misconceptions: treats 0 as a power of two
uses n/2 with truncation on odds
strategies: Handle n<=0, n==1, odd, even as your four branches.
Trace 12 to see the false path.
common_mistakes: Recursing on n-2 instead of n/2.
entries.world_effect: The charger accepts only clean power-of-two cells; the sorter now flags the rest.
entries.post_solve: Recursion mirrors the DEFINITION of a structure — here, repeated halving.

entries.title: Badge anagram check
entries.micro_lesson: Count letters with a map (char -> count); two strings match iff their count-maps match.
entries.prompt: Return whether the two badge codes are anagrams (same letters, same counts).
misconceptions: counts letters of one string only
strategies: Build one count-map per string, or +1/-1 in a single map.
Different lengths can never be anagrams.
entries.world_effect: Forged badges with shuffled letters stop fooling the checkpoint scanner.
entries.post_solve: Maps turn 'compare arrangements' into 'compare counts' — order stops mattering.

entries.title: First duplicated supply tag
entries.micro_lesson: A 'seen' set/map answers 'have I met this before?' in one step per element.
entries.prompt: Return the first tag value whose second occurrence appears earliest; -1 if all tags are unique.
misconceptions: returns the index instead of the value
strategies: Walk left to right; check 'seen' BEFORE inserting.
Return -1 only after the loop finishes.
entries.world_effect: The intake scanner flags double-logged crates the moment they pass.
entries.post_solve: Sets/maps buy O(1) membership — the difference between one pass and a nested scan.

entries.title: Count distinct supply types
entries.micro_lesson: A set is a map without values: insert everything, its size is your distinct count.
entries.prompt: Return how many DIFFERENT supply type-codes appear in the manifest.
strategies: Insert all, then read the size.
Decide the empty answer (0) before coding.
entries.world_effect: The depot board shows real variety, not raw crate count — rationing gets smarter.
entries.post_solve: When only membership matters, reach for a set before a list.

entries.title: Most requested supply
entries.micro_lesson: Count with a map, then take the key with the largest count — the histogram pattern.
entries.prompt: Return the value that appears most often (tests guarantee a unique winner).
misconceptions: returns the count instead of the value
tracks only the last element's count
strategies: Two phases: build counts, then scan for the max.
Track best-value and best-count together.
entries.world_effect: The requisition board reorders itself around what survivors actually ask for.
entries.post_solve: Histograms are the workhorse of data questions: count first, ask second.

entries.title: Densest letter in the callsign
entries.micro_lesson: Strings are sequences too — the same char->count map answers density questions.
entries.worked_example: mississippi: i x4, s x4? s appears 4, i appears 4 -> max 4.
entries.prompt: Return the highest occurrence count of any single character in the callsign (0 for empty).
misconceptions: returns the character, not the count
strategies: Guard the empty case first.
One pass to count; one pass (or running max) to answer.
common_mistakes: Counting bytes vs characters confusion (tests are ASCII).
entries.world_effect: The cipher desk spots repeated-letter callsigns that jam the radio codes.
entries.post_solve: Map thinking transfers across types: ints, strings, anything hashable.

entries.title: Manifest linear search
entries.micro_lesson: Linear search: scan left to right, return the FIRST index that matches, -1 when absent.
entries.prompt: Return the first index of target in the manifest, or -1 if it is missing.
misconceptions: returns the value instead of the index
strategies: Return INSIDE the loop on match.
The -1 belongs after the loop, not in it.
common_mistakes: Returning early with -1 on the first mismatch.
entries.world_effect: Crate lookups stop tearing the depot apart — the finder points at one shelf.
entries.post_solve: Every fancier search is judged against this baseline: O(n), first match, -1 contract.

entries.title: Is the evac route sorted?
entries.micro_lesson: Sortedness is a PAIRWISE property: every adjacent pair must be non-decreasing.
entries.prompt: Return whether the route's waypoint ids are in non-decreasing order.
strategies: Loop to len-2 comparing i and i+1.
One bad pair ends it — return false immediately.
common_mistakes: Index out of range at the last pair.
entries.world_effect: The nav computer trusts the route and unlocks fast-travel along it.
entries.post_solve: Binary search (next door) is only legal on data that passes THIS check.

entries.title: Second-strongest signal
entries.micro_lesson: Track TWO running values (best, second) in one pass — no full sort needed.
entries.prompt: Return the second-largest DISTINCT value (tests guarantee at least two distinct values).
misconceptions: returns the second element, not second largest
duplicates of the max shadow the runner-up
strategies: Update (best, second) carefully in that order.
Skip values equal to best when filling second.
entries.world_effect: The relay auto-selects a backup mast the instant the primary drops.
entries.post_solve: Partial answers (top-k) rarely need a full sort — cheaper invariants win.

entries.title: Crates under the threshold
entries.micro_lesson: Counting with a predicate: scan once, +1 whenever the condition holds.
entries.prompt: Return how many crate weights are strictly below the carry limit.
strategies: Strictly below means <, test the boundary value.
Accumulate a count, not a list.
common_mistakes: Counting values equal to the limit.
Returning early after the first match.
entries.world_effect: The loadmaster instantly knows what one runner can carry through the breach.
entries.post_solve: On SORTED data this becomes binary search for the boundary — tier 10 energy.

entries.title: Refactor: charge formula
entries.micro_lesson: Same spec as your tier-3 loop — but n*(n+1)/2 answers in ONE step. Complexity is a design choice.
entries.prompt: Return 1+2+...+n WITHOUT a loop, using the closed-form formula.
misconceptions: divides before multiplying with integer types
strategies: Multiply first, then halve — one of n, n+1 is even.
Check n=1 gives 1.
common_mistakes: Float division leaving .0 artifacts in typed languages.
entries.world_effect: The generator charges instantly now — the crank montage is over.
entries.post_solve: You just refactored O(n) to O(1). Same contract, different cost — THAT is engineering.

entries.title: Pair-sum lockout
entries.micro_lesson: Nested scan is O(n^2); a 'seen' set asking for (target - value) makes it one pass.
entries.worked_example: target 9: see 2, need 7... later meet 7 -> true.
entries.prompt: Return whether any two DIFFERENT positions sum to the target code.
misconceptions: checks pairs only once left-to-right... and misses none — but n^2
strategies: For each value, ask: have I SEEN its complement?
Insert AFTER checking to avoid self-pairing.
common_mistakes: Counting v + v = target with one occurrence.
entries.world_effect: The vault stops brute-forcing pairs — the door answers before the horde arrives.
entries.post_solve: The map/set from tier 8 just accelerated a tier-9 search. Concepts compound.

entries.title: Longest stable power run
entries.micro_lesson: One pass, two counters: current-run length and best-so-far. Reset on change, never look back.
entries.prompt: Return the length of the longest run of equal consecutive readings (0 for empty).
misconceptions: compares to the first element instead of the previous
strategies: Update best INSIDE the loop (or once after).
Empty input first: define the answer as 0.
common_mistakes: Missing the last run when the array ends mid-run.
Starting current at 0 with non-empty input.
entries.world_effect: The grid report highlights the steadiest generator — that's the one worth guarding.
entries.post_solve: Sliding one-pass state machines beat re-scanning windows — linear beats quadratic again.

entries.title: Best evac trade window
entries.micro_lesson: Track the minimum so far; the best gain at each step is value - minSoFar. One pass, O(1) space.
entries.prompt: Return the best possible later-minus-earlier gain in the supply price list (0 if it only falls).
misconceptions: returns negative best on falling data
strategies: Carry minSoFar; compare-and-update both values each step.
Falling-only input must yield 0.
common_mistakes: Using global max/min pair regardless of order.
entries.world_effect: The trader NPC finally quotes fair barter windows instead of gut feelings.
entries.post_solve: You reduced all pairs O(n^2) to a single sweep with one remembered fact. Capstone complete.

entries.title: Refactor: callsign word flip
entries.micro_lesson: Refactor pipelines: split -> reverse -> join beats index juggling for clarity AND correctness.
entries.prompt: Return the callsign with its WORDS in reverse order (single spaces, no leading/trailing).
strategies: Think in stages: split, reverse, join.
Test the single-word case.
entries.world_effect: Reversed callsigns unlock the mirrored checkpoint's challenge-response.
entries.post_solve: Readable pipelines are refactoring's gift: each stage testable, no index arithmetic.
